claim: An insertion effect's output level byte is a multiplier stored as a whole number over a hundred and twenty-seven, and that multiplier is not the byte. Every one of the hundred and twenty-five settings the run could read returns a gain that sits on the 1/127 grid: a median 0.0225 of a step away, against 0.2185 for the next best denominator of the sixty-one asked and 0.25 for a number that sat on no grid at all. What the entries are is a curve and not a formula -- the multiplier is three quarters of the byte over the bottom quarter of the range and rises to the byte itself at the top, and no law in the catalogue crosses that. The byte read straight as the multiplier is out by a median 1.61 decibels and by 3.53 at setting 9.
named: a stored table of seven-bit multipliers, one per setting
adds: The record says how loud the take was at each of the hundred and twenty-eight settings, and says in as many words that no law, no curve and no quantum is in it. Nothing in it says the gains land on a grid, which grid, that the grid means the numbers were stored, or that the byte is not the multiplier. That is the whole of what is added, and it is added by scanning every nearby denominator and by holding four candidate laws against the same readings.
refutedBy: A setting whose multiplier sits a third of a step or more from the 1/127 grid while its take is well clear of the chain's silence, which no admitted setting does -- the worst is 0.24 of a step at setting 122, where one step is 0.068 decibels and the run resolves 0.01. Or another denominator scanned over the same settings coming closer, which none of the sixty-one does by a factor of ten. Or a level byte on another type returning multipliers that sit on no grid at all, which would make this a property of one effect rather than of how a gain is stored.

whatItWouldChange.what: Anything rendering an SC-series insertion effect at a level other than 127.
whatItWouldChange.how: A renderer using the byte as the multiplier is three and a half decibels loud at the bottom of the byte and a decibel and a half loud through the middle of it, in the direction that matters: it is loud where a part was meant to sit back. The table is a hundred and twenty-eight bytes and removes all of it.

eraPriors.claim: A gain is one number, so a table of a hundred and twenty-eight of them costs a hundred and twenty-eight bytes and nothing about the period argues for a runtime formula instead.
eraPriors.why: This is the opposite of what the same period implies about a frequency parameter, and the difference is what is stored per entry. A filter entry is a set of coefficients, so entries are expensive and the table is short -- sixteen of them, which is the finding on 40 03 07. A gain entry is one multiplier, so the table can be as long as the byte and the designer is free to put any curve in it.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The measured multipliers followed a law cheap enough to evaluate at speed, which would say the table was not written even though it could have been. Four such laws were held against the sweep and the best is out by a median 1.61 decibels.

eraPriors.claim: A denominator of a hundred and twenty-seven says the numbers were stored rather than computed.
eraPriors.why: Dividing by 127 is not arithmetic a fixed-point part of this period does per sample; dividing by 128 is a shift. A table written so that the top of the byte reaches exactly unity has 127 as its denominator for free, because the table is the division. So the denominator is not only a quantum, it is a statement about where the arithmetic happened.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The grid had turned out to be 128 or a power of two, which the scan asked and which sits with every other losing denominator at a fifth of a step away.

community.claim: In the same reverse-engineering record this archive already cites for the frequency class, a gain parameter of that rendering indexes a stored table rather than being used as a multiplier, and a byte past the table's end is ignored rather than clamped. That is the same shape as the claim here and it is not the same parameter: what was read there is an equaliser's gain in decibels, printed -12 - +12 and holding a handful of entries, while this is an effect's output level, printed 0 - 127. So it carries the claim no further than the era prior above already does -- that a maker of this line stored gains rather than computing them -- and it says nothing about the denominator, about a table this long, or about what the entries are. The two were read in the same session and this claim was made from the sweep first.
community.source: The TabulaSonora project's reverse-engineering record of the Roland SOUND Canvas VA voice: docs/FINDINGS.md in its spec repository, and the insertion-effect source of its NativeTS engine. Read 2026-09-13.

alternatives.reading: The multiplier is the byte over 128 rather than over 127, which is the divide the part can actually do.
The grid is 1/127 because the reading is, and not because the unit is. Something in the capture or the analysis could quantise a level to one part in 127.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: Nothing in the chain has 127 in it. The take is 24-bit at 48 kHz, the level is a sum of squares over eight seconds published to two decimal places in decibels, and neither has a quantum near one part in a hundred and twenty-seven of amplitude. If the reading imposed the grid it would impose it on every sweep, and the frequency sweeps of the same session return levels that sit a fifth of a step from it.

alternatives.reading: The curve is a law after all, and the catalogue is missing it.

separatedBy.observable: Whether the same address on another type returns the same hundred and twenty-eight multipliers.
separatedBy.what_the_run_returned: It was run. Eleven settings over 26.5 dB on 01 40 agree with 01 00 to a worst 0.04 dB. That refutes a curve computed per type and it separates a table from a law by nothing at all, because both predicted exactly this.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: A law that returns these hundred and twenty-eight numbers and a table holding them differ in where the numbers come from and in nothing that comes out, so no reading of this unit's output can tell them apart. The class does not rest on the difference: what is claimed is the multiplier and its quantum, and both readings give the same multiplier. What argues for the table is the era and not a measurement -- 128 entries cost 128 bytes -- and a prior may carry a claim and may not close one, so this stays open and says why.

alternatives.reading: The curve is what a type carries whose output is proportional to its input. Both types it has been read on are that: four filter sections, and a modulator with a delay line. A stage that saturates has a reason to scale its own output that neither of those has, and the byte is printed as that stage's output level.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The run it asked for was made, twice over, and the curve did not move. At the settings both drives admit the two agree to a worst 0.05 dB where one of these readings resolves 0.166, and each agrees with the first type to a worst 0.04 and 0.04 dB. A level the drive stage applied itself would have to move when the drive does; this one does not move at all, so the byte is applied after the stage and what it holds is the class's curve and not the stage's.

separatedBy.observable: Whether the same address on a type with a drive stage returns the same hundred and twenty-eight multipliers, and whether what it returns moves when the drive does.

predicts.the stored table, applied after the stag: The multipliers the two linear types returned, and the same curve at both drives. A gain applied after a stage cannot know how hard the stage was being driven.
predicts.a scaling the drive stage does itself: A curve that leaves the linear types' somewhere, and leaves itself between the two drives -- a level folded into a saturating stage is a level whose effect depends on what is arriving at it.

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: 0.166 dB, the spread of one setting's own repeats on the second type. What has to clear it is one entry of the table, and how large that is depends on where in the byte it is read: 0.07 dB at the top of the range, 0.27 at setting 32 and 1.16 at setting 8. So the settings are weighted to the bottom, and the figure the margin is taken at is the coarsest of them that is still a reading.

run.why_this_type: It is the only family on this unit with a nonlinearity, and it is also the loudest thing the class can be read through -- which decides how far down the byte the reading reaches, because the stored curve and every law in the catalogue part company at the bottom and a setting is admitted only where it stands over the same chain's floor. The first type read reached setting 3 and the second only 8. Which type is loudest was measured rather than assumed: every candidate went through one short take of its own, and this one came back 5.7 dB over the first type at drive 0 and 2.9 at drive 96, against the second type by 12.0 and 9.2, and against the delay that looked like the obvious third type by 7.6 and 4.8 -- that delay being 1.9 dB quieter than the first type and so the worst of the candidates for this reading. Those are differences between types in one reading and not levels over the admission rule's floor, which is a different reading and a different number; what transfers between the two is the ordering and not the size. It also prints no balance, so nothing of the signal goes past the row being read.
run.why_two_drives: A curve measured once is a curve, and nothing in it says where in the chain it was applied. Two drives of the one stage that makes this type different say whether the byte is applied after that stage or inside it, which is the half of the question a third type alone cannot reach.

stimulus: A held note through the effect, read as the level of the whole take against the run's own repeats of one setting.
domain.outside: The absolute gain, which the bypass control says this chain cannot give. Every type except 01 00. Setting 0, which is the effect off rather than a quiet setting of it. What the byte does to anything but the level -- a multiplier that changed the shape as well would not show in a figure that is one number per take.

residual.unit: decibels between the level a candidate law says and the level read
residual.why: the signed median swings 3.529 dB across the settings and 0 dB across the readings within one, against the run's own floor of 0.1357 dB

gates.name: gross
gates.why: The median residual over the span the effect commands, taken as the worst of the records scored. A rejection bound and not a target: below it the residual is reported and never optimised, because no candidate is decided by it.

gates.name: qualitative
gates.why: Properties the unit's readings have that the model's readings must have too. No arithmetic over a residual rescues a model that cuts where the unit boosts.

gates.name: power
gates.why: The runner-up in the catalogue, scored on the same records, and whether it leans or contradicts a property where the winner does neither. The decoy is not chosen -- it is whichever candidate came second, so a strawman cannot be put up in its place. A class holding one candidate is a catalogue that is unfinished, which is a finding and not a pass.

gates.name: breakdown
gates.why: A point worse than 0.5 of the span is a failure at that point rather than error at it. A residual that leans with the setting or with frequency is pointing at a structure the model does not have; one that does not is pointing at the room and the converters, and is not made smaller by anything this project can do.

compared_against.why_not_a_filter: The set is one record and it was chosen rather than generated: the only sweep of this address that asked every one of the hundred and twenty-eight settings. That is a property of how a record was taken and not of where it is filed, so no filter over the index picks it out -- the same address on this type has another record that moved the byte at six settings while reading a corner, and it is not a reading of this class. The second type's sweep is held against this one record to record, which is stated under a_second_type rather than folded in here, because two measurements compared to each other with no model between them are not a model's comparison set.

reproduces.read_as: This block is the law race and not the claim. What it says is that the best formula in the catalogue breaks down: the byte read straight as the multiplier passes the gross gate at a twenty-second of the span and then leans, because it is out by three and a half decibels at the bottom of the byte and by a third of one at the top. The candidate that is the readout is not in this race -- its entries are the measurement, so a ranking that included it would rank the measurement first and call that a finding.

extra.key: a note on what was left out
extra.text: The candidate whose entries are the measurement was written, scored and then taken out of the ranking, and the first run of this class left it in -- where it came first with a residual of two ten-thousandths of the span and the four gates returned `reproduces`. That verdict was the measurement agreeing with itself. It is the same failure the equaliser's centre frequencies already had in this archive, where a model carrying twelve measured settings and interpolating between them was published as a law, and it is worth naming twice because it does not look like a failure from inside: every gate passes, the residual is beautiful, and nothing in the numbers says the model was copied from the thing it is being held against. What separates a readout from a law is whether it could have come out wrong, and a table with a free entry per setting could not. So the readout is published as a readout, its residual is reported as the reading's own rounding error, and the claim rests on the one thing a free table cannot arrange -- that the unrounded measurements sit on a grid, scanned against every nearby denominator.
